Analytical stance under test: warranty-support-and-vendor-attestation-first - an artefact that no party will support is a liability the benchmark does not price.

Falsifiable hypothesis H200a: every component in the quantized serving path is covered by the same support commitments as the baseline path, testable by enumerating the kernels, engine version, quantization library and checkpoint provenance in each arm and checking each against the applicable support matrix or contract. If any element in the quantized arm falls outside supported configurations, incident response for that path has no escalation route and that cost belongs in the comparison.

Production serving decisions are made under support obligations, not only under performance numbers. A quantized path frequently pulls in a different kernel family, an experimental engine flag, a community quantization library or a re-derived checkpoint whose provenance differs from the vendor-signed baseline, and each of those can move the deployment outside the configurations any party has committed to support. The failure mode is not a slow response, it is an unresolvable one: an incident traced to a kernel in an unsupported path has no escalation route and no fix timeline, and the team absorbs the outage duration. Enumerate the path explicitly per arm, listing engine build, kernel implementations actually selected at runtime rather than nominally available, quantization library and version, and checkpoint provenance with its signing or hashing chain, then check each element against the applicable support matrix and record where the arms diverge. Where the quantized arm relies on an unsupported element, the comparison must either price the self-support burden, meaning the engineering capacity to debug kernels in-house and the expected time to resolution, or scope the adoption to a tier where that risk is acceptable. There is a related licensing question on re-derived artefacts: producing a quantized checkpoint creates a derivative whose redistribution and use terms follow from the base model's licence, and that must be confirmed rather than assumed. Boundary condition: an entirely self-supported stack with in-house kernel expertise has no external support matrix to violate, and this axis reduces to internal on-call capacity, which should still be stated rather than left implicit. ESTIMATE: expected unsupported-path cost scales with incident rate times mean self-resolution time, and self-resolution time for kernel-level defects is typically much longer than for configuration defects; derivation is multiplying incident frequency by resolution duration under each support regime, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED.



--- Shared substrate (identical across this study, stated once so the stance above is the only variable) ---

Mechanism. Weight-only quantization (WOQ) reduces the BYTES OF WEIGHTS READ PER FORWARD PASS. It therefore helps only where the kernel is memory-bandwidth bound, which in LLM serving means small-batch autoregressive decode. Prefill is compute bound; dequantization adds arithmetic there, so TTFT is flat or slightly worse. As batch size rises, decode GEMMs become compute bound too and the advantage decays monotonically toward 1.0x. Any claim of a uniform speedup across the concurrency range is mechanically wrong and should be treated as an instrumentation bug until explained.

Byte-count ceiling (ESTIMATE, derivation inline, not a throughput result). A 9B-parameter model in BF16 is 9e9 x 2 B = 18 GB of weights. INT4 with group-128 FP16 scale and zero point costs about 0.5 + ~0.06 B/param, i.e. ~5.0-5.3 GB. Ratio ~3.2-3.6x. This is pure byte counting with no kernel-efficiency model and no attention or KV traffic included; it is an upper bound on batch-1 decode speedup ONLY. Applying Amdahl with a decode-weight-read fraction f: f=0.4 bounds end-to-end gain near 1.33x, f=0.8 near 2.1x (ESTIMATE).

Mandatory two-arm-plus-one design. Run the quantized configuration TWICE: (a) with KV cache block count clamped to the BF16 baseline's block count, which isolates the kernel/bandwidth effect; (b) at native capacity, which shows the deployable benefit. Freed HBM becomes additional KV blocks and raises throughput by batching alone. If the clamped arm is flat, the honest conclusion is "we bought KV headroom", and tuning KV settings on the BF16 arm must be priced as the cheaper alternative before shipping a second numeric path.

Arm identity is frozen and hashed. Checkpoint hash, bit width, group size, symmetric/asymmetric, outlier or mixed-precision policy, calibration dataset hash, library and engine build, TP/PP layout, activation precision, KV precision, block size, max_num_seqs, max_model_len, chunked-prefill state, speculative-decoding state. The configuration symmetric difference between arms must be exactly the bit-width fields; anything else invalidates the comparison. Weight-only means weight-only: "INT4 plus FP8 KV" is two experiments, and the KV change usually explains most of the throughput delta while none of the quality delta gets attributed correctly.

Comparison point. Compare arms at the intersection of each arm's own latency-throughput frontier with the p95 SLO, never at a fixed batch size; the two arms have different optimal batch sizes, and fixed-batch comparison is the single most common way these studies mislead. Cost unit is GPU-seconds per 1,000 output tokens at that fixed p95 SLO, converted to currency last.

Measurement protocol. At least five concurrency points, at least three repeats per point, steady state with a fixed warmup-exclusion rule, greedy decoding and fixed seed for quality, bootstrap 95% CIs on ABSOLUTE quality deltas. Quality is sliced: long context, structured/JSON output, code, math, safety and refusal behaviour; aggregate scores can stay flat while repetition or truncation degrades, so sampled side-by-side output diffs are part of the evidence, not a nicety. A BF16-vs-BF16 A/A control across seeds and physical GPUs establishes the noise floor that any claimed delta must clear.

Confounders to control and report. Autotune cache warmth; clock and thermal drift over long runs; asymmetric telemetry overhead; prefill/decode mix drift between arms; silent kernel fallback to a dequantize-then-GEMM path (dump per-layer kernel names and timings and diff the arms - a null result with a fallback in the logs is a tooling defect, not a verdict on the method); calibration-set leakage into the eval set, disproved by hash comparison; library defaults silently changing group size across versions.

Evidence required before any decision. Per-request raw records (arrival, TTFT, per-token timestamps, output length, status); per-layer kernel name and achieved-bandwidth traces for both arms; the arm configuration manifest with hashes; per-slice quality scores with CIs plus raw generations; the HBM ledger with KV blocks as the residual and a measured high-water mark; the A/A noise-floor numbers; and matched-window fleet GPU-hour and token accounting, because benchmarks propose and production billing disposes.

Rollback gates, pre-committed. Revert if p95 TTFT or TPOT exceeds SLO at target concurrency; if any eval slice falls more than 1.0 point absolute with a 95% CI excluding zero; if structured-output compliance falls more than 2 points; if measured cost improvement is under 25%; if preemption or recompute rates rise without explanation; or if kernel-fallback evidence appears, in which case fix the tooling and re-run rather than concluding anything. Keep the BF16 arm warm and routable throughout so rollback is a routing flip rather than a redeploy, and rehearse the revert once before the canary.

Declared unknowns. Kernel efficiency on the specific shapes and TP degree in use, per-layer sensitivity of the specific checkpoint, and the production decode-token fraction are all MEASURED quantities in this design; none of them are asserted here. Every number above is labelled ESTIMATE and carries its derivation.

corrected_answer:
Analytical stance under test: latency-metric-decomposition-first - TTFT and TPOT are governed by different bottlenecks and the two parallelism axes move them in opposite directions.

Falsifiable hypothesis H200c: for the stated latency target, the layout that minimises TTFT also minimises TPOT, testable by measuring TTFT and TPOT separately under both layouts across the load sweep and checking whether the two metrics select the same arm. If they select different arms, the deployment must state which metric the SLO is denominated in before any recommendation is valid, because no layout wins both.

Collapsing serving latency into a single number is the fastest way to a wrong parallelism decision, because prefill and decode are governed by different bottlenecks. TTFT is dominated by prefill, which is compute-bound and parallelises well across tensor shards, so tensor parallelism reduces TTFT roughly in proportion to the added devices minus the per-layer collective overhead. Pipeline parallelism does not help TTFT for a single request at all: the request must traverse every stage sequentially, and the stage transfers add to the path, so PP's TTFT is at best equal to the single-device case and typically slightly worse. TPOT behaves differently. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound on weight reads, and tensor parallelism divides the weight bytes each device must read per step, so TPOT also improves under TP, but the per-layer collective is now a larger fraction of a much shorter step, so the improvement saturates and can invert past a TP degree where collective latency exceeds the compute it hid. Under PP, a single request's TPOT is the sum of stage decode times plus transfers, so it does not improve with more stages, though aggregate token throughput does once enough concurrent requests fill the stages. Measure both metrics separately across the load sweep, report them as separate curves, and require the SLO document to state which one it constrains. Boundary condition: workloads with very long prompts and short outputs are TTFT-dominated and favour TP strongly; workloads with short prompts and long outputs are TPOT-dominated and the TP degree must be tuned against collective overhead rather than maximised. ESTIMATE: TP speedup on both metrics is bounded above by the TP degree and reduced by the per-layer collective term, so the marginal benefit of each doubling shrinks and eventually turns negative; derivation is dividing per-device work by the shard count while holding the collective count per layer fixed, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED.

--- Shared substrate (identical across this study, stated once so the stance above is the only variable) ---

Mechanism. Tensor parallelism (TP) splits every layer's weight matrices across devices, so each token's forward pass requires a collective (all-reduce or reduce-scatter/all-gather) at every TP-sharded block. TP therefore reduces per-device weight bytes and per-device FLOPs for a single request, and it lowers single-request latency, but it pays a collective on the critical path of every layer of every step. Pipeline parallelism (PP) splits the model by layer depth across devices, so a single request traverses stages sequentially and its latency is the sum of stage times plus point-to-point transfers; PP's inter-stage traffic is small (one activation tensor per boundary) but a single in-flight request leaves all but one stage idle. The mechanical consequence for a latency-sensitive service is asymmetric: TP reduces the latency of one request; PP does not, and only recovers device utilisation by keeping multiple microbatches in flight, which is a throughput mechanism, not a latency mechanism.

Boundary conditions that decide the answer. (1) Interconnect class within a TP group. TP is viable only when the devices in a TP group share a high-bandwidth, low-latency link; across a slower fabric the per-layer collective dominates and TP latency degrades rather than improves. (2) Whether the model fits. If per-device memory cannot hold weights plus KV cache plus activation workspace at the target context length and concurrency, some sharding is mandatory and the question becomes which axis, not whether. (3) Offered concurrency. At concurrency 1 PP is nearly pure loss; at high sustained concurrency PP's bubbles fill and its throughput per device can exceed TP's because it pays no per-layer collective. (4) Whether the latency target is on TTFT, TPOT, or end-to-end, since prefill is compute-bound and decode is bandwidth-bound and the two axes affect them differently.

Assumptions that must be stated before any recommendation. Model parameter count and dtype; per-device memory capacity; target context length and output length distribution; the p95 or p99 latency target and which metric it is denominated in; offered load in requests per second and its burstiness; intra-node interconnect type and topology, and whether any parallel group would cross a node boundary; the serving engine and its scheduler mode (continuous batching, chunked prefill); and whether the deployment must tolerate device failure without full restart. A recommendation issued without these is not an engineering answer.

Falsifiability and controlled experiment. The comparison must fix the model checkpoint hash, the request trace, the tokenizer, the sampling policy (greedy, fixed seed, for quality) and the total device count, and vary only the parallelism layout. Sweep offered load across at least five points spanning the production level through saturation, at least three repeats per point, steady state with a declared warmup-exclusion rule, and report full latency-versus-load curves with per-arm knees rather than single-point numbers. Run an A/A control (identical layout, different seeds and different physical devices) first to establish the noise floor that any claimed delta must clear.

Evidence required before any decision. Per-request raw records with arrival timestamp, TTFT, per-token timestamps, output length and terminal status; per-step timeline profiles giving collective duration, exposed non-overlapped communication time, point-to-point stage transfer time, and per-rank straggler distribution; the memory ledger per device with weights, KV blocks and activation workspace itemised plus a measured high-water mark; the achieved KV block count and preemption or recompute rate per arm, since a layout that leaves less KV headroom silently caps concurrency; the interconnect topology as enumerated by the platform rather than assumed; and a reconfiguration drill measuring time to recover from a single device failure under each layout.

Confounders to control and report. Autotune and kernel-cache warmth, which favours whichever arm ran second; clock and thermal drift over long sweeps; asymmetric telemetry overhead between arms; NUMA placement and whether any parallel group crosses a socket or node boundary; scheduler differences such as chunked prefill being enabled by default at one layout and not the other; and PP microbatch or TP group size being left at engine defaults rather than tuned per arm, which compares a tuned configuration against an untuned one.

Rollback gates, pre-committed. Revert if p95 TTFT or TPOT exceeds the SLO at target concurrency; if achieved throughput per device at the SLO-constrained operating point is worse than the incumbent; if preemption or KV recompute rates rise without an explanation traced to a named mechanism; if any quality slice regresses with a 95% CI excluding zero, which would indicate a numerics or sharding-correctness defect rather than a performance trade; or if the failure-recovery drill exceeds the availability budget. Keep the incumbent layout warm and routable so rollback is a routing flip, and rehearse the revert once before the canary.

Achieved collective bandwidth on the specific shapes and topology, the production prefill-to-decode token ratio, the real burstiness of offered load, and per-stage load balance under the actual layer partition are all MEASURED quantities in this design and are not asserted here. Analytical stance under test: numerical-equivalence-and-sharding-correctness-first - a parallelism change is supposed to be quality-neutral, and that neutrality is a testable claim rather than a guarantee.

Falsifiable hypothesis H200j: outputs are numerically equivalent within a stated tolerance across the two layouts under greedy decoding with a fixed seed and identical inputs, testable by running a fixed prompt set through both layouts and comparing generated token sequences and logits. If outputs diverge beyond floating-point reassociation tolerance, there is a sharding or collective-correctness defect and no performance number from either arm is trustworthy until it is resolved.

Unlike quantization, changing the parallelism layout is not supposed to change what the model computes, which makes numerical comparison a correctness test rather than a quality trade-off. That test is worth running because the layouts differ in real ways that can break equivalence. Collective reductions change the order of floating-point accumulation, and floating-point addition is not associative, so bitwise identity is not expected; small logit differences are normal and can flip a token at a near-tie, which then diverges the whole continuation. Distinguish that benign mechanism from genuine defects by comparing logit distributions on the first generated position rather than only the final text, since a reassociation difference shows as a tiny logit perturbation while a sharding bug, a wrong rank mapping, a mis-partitioned attention head group or an incorrectly replicated normalisation parameter shows as a large one. Run a fixed prompt set under greedy decoding with a fixed seed through both layouts, report first-position logit differences and the position at which text first diverges, and treat large early divergence as a blocking defect. Long-context and structured-output slices deserve extra weight because attention-head sharding and position-handling bugs frequently only manifest past a certain sequence length or with particular masking patterns. Boundary condition: with sampling enabled, seeds do not guarantee identical streams across layouts because the number and order of random draws can differ, so the equivalence test must be run under greedy decoding and the sampling path validated separately by distributional comparison. ESTIMATE: benign reassociation differences are on the order of floating-point epsilon accumulated over the reduction tree depth, which is far smaller than the logit gaps that separate confident predictions, so a large early logit difference indicates a defect rather than reassociation; derivation is comparing accumulated rounding magnitude against typical logit separation, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED.

--- Shared substrate (identical across this study, stated once so the stance above is the only variable) ---

Mechanism. Tensor parallelism (TP) splits every layer's weight matrices across devices, so each token's forward pass requires a collective (all-reduce or reduce-scatter/all-gather) at every TP-sharded block. TP therefore reduces per-device weight bytes and per-device FLOPs for a single request, and it lowers single-request latency, but it pays a collective on the critical path of every layer of every step. Pipeline parallelism (PP) splits the model by layer depth across devices, so a single request traverses stages sequentially and its latency is the sum of stage times plus point-to-point transfers; PP's inter-stage traffic is small (one activation tensor per boundary) but a single in-flight request leaves all but one stage idle. The mechanical consequence for a latency-sensitive service is asymmetric: TP reduces the latency of one request; PP does not, and only recovers device utilisation by keeping multiple microbatches in flight, which is a throughput mechanism, not a latency mechanism.

Boundary conditions that decide the answer. (1) Interconnect class within a TP group. TP is viable only when the devices in a TP group share a high-bandwidth, low-latency link; across a slower fabric the per-layer collective dominates and TP latency degrades rather than improves. (2) Whether the model fits. If per-device memory cannot hold weights plus KV cache plus activation workspace at the target context length and concurrency, some sharding is mandatory and the question becomes which axis, not whether. (3) Offered concurrency. At concurrency 1 PP is nearly pure loss; at high sustained concurrency PP's bubbles fill and its throughput per device can exceed TP's because it pays no per-layer collective. (4) Whether the latency target is on TTFT, TPOT, or end-to-end, since prefill is compute-bound and decode is bandwidth-bound and the two axes affect them differently.

Assumptions that must be stated before any recommendation. Model parameter count and dtype; per-device memory capacity; target context length and output length distribution; the p95 or p99 latency target and which metric it is denominated in; offered load in requests per second and its burstiness; intra-node interconnect type and topology, and whether any parallel group would cross a node boundary; the serving engine and its scheduler mode (continuous batching, chunked prefill); and whether the deployment must tolerate device failure without full restart. A recommendation issued without these is not an engineering answer.

Falsifiability and controlled experiment. The comparison must fix the model checkpoint hash, the request trace, the tokenizer, the sampling policy (greedy, fixed seed, for quality) and the total device count, and vary only the parallelism layout. Sweep offered load across at least five points spanning the production level through saturation, at least three repeats per point, steady state with a declared warmup-exclusion rule, and report full latency-versus-load curves with per-arm knees rather than single-point numbers. Run an A/A control (identical layout, different seeds and different physical devices) first to establish the noise floor that any claimed delta must clear.

Evidence required before any decision. Per-request raw records with arrival timestamp, TTFT, per-token timestamps, output length and terminal status; per-step timeline profiles giving collective duration, exposed non-overlapped communication time, point-to-point stage transfer time, and per-rank straggler distribution; the memory ledger per device with weights, KV blocks and activation workspace itemised plus a measured high-water mark; the achieved KV block count and preemption or recompute rate per arm, since a layout that leaves less KV headroom silently caps concurrency; the interconnect topology as enumerated by the platform rather than assumed; and a reconfiguration drill measuring time to recover from a single device failure under each layout.

Confounders to control and report. Autotune and kernel-cache warmth, which favours whichever arm ran second; clock and thermal drift over long sweeps; asymmetric telemetry overhead between arms; NUMA placement and whether any parallel group crosses a socket or node boundary; scheduler differences such as chunked prefill being enabled by default at one layout and not the other; and PP microbatch or TP group size being left at engine defaults rather than tuned per arm, which compares a tuned configuration against an untuned one.

Rollback gates, pre-committed. Revert if p95 TTFT or TPOT exceeds the SLO at target concurrency; if achieved throughput per device at the SLO-constrained operating point is worse than the incumbent; if preemption or KV recompute rates rise without an explanation traced to a named mechanism; if any quality slice regresses with a 95% CI excluding zero, which would indicate a numerics or sharding-correctness defect rather than a performance trade; or if the failure-recovery drill exceeds the availability budget. Keep the incumbent layout warm and routable so rollback is a routing flip, and rehearse the revert once before the canary.

Declared unknowns. Achieved collective bandwidth on the specific shapes and topology, the production prefill-to-decode token ratio, the real burstiness of offered load, and per-stage load balance under the actual layer partition are all MEASURED quantities in this design and are not asserted here. Every number in the stance above is labelled ESTIMATE with its derivation inline.
